summary.text: After expanding the coefficient as a double sum, Lucas’s parity criterion turns oddness of its two binomial factors into disjointness conditions on binary digits; these conditions show that every odd summand indexed by \((n,k)\), with \(j=(N-n(k+1))/(n+1)\), is paired involutively with the summand indexed by \((j+k,k)\). A fixed point forces \(j=0\) and \(n=k\), hence \(N=k(k+1)\); away from such a fixed point all odd summands cancel in pairs modulo \(2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge 0}x^n\frac{(1+x^n)^n}{(1-x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
     =\sum_{N\ge 0}a(N)x^N.
\]
We prove that if \(a(N)\) is odd, then \(N=k(k+1)\) for some \(k\ge 0\).

We first record the parity criterion for binomial coefficients that will be used throughout.

For nonnegative integers \(u,v\), write their binary expansions as
\[
u=\sum_{r\ge0}u_r2^r,\qquad v=\sum_{r\ge0}v_r2^r,
\]
where every \(u_r,v_r\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). Then
\[
\binom uv\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v_r\le u_r\text{ for every }r.
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, over the field with two elements,
\[
(1+X)^{2^r}=1+X^{2^r}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(1+X)^u=\prod_{r:u_r=1}(1+X^{2^r}).
\]
The coefficient of \(X^v\) in this product is \(1\) exactly when each binary digit occurring in \(v\) is among the binary digits occurring in \(u\). Since that coefficient is \(\binom uv\) reduced modulo \(2\), this proves (1).

We shall say that two nonnegative integers are binary-disjoint, and write \(r\perp s\), when they have no binary position at which both have digit \(1\). Equivalently, their bitwise AND is zero. A useful consequence of (1) is
\[
\binom{r+s}{s}\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\perp s.
\tag{2}
\]
To see this directly, if \(r\perp s\), their binary addition has no carries, so \(r+s\) is their bitwise OR and therefore contains every \(1\)-digit of \(s\). Criterion (1) gives oddness. Conversely, if \(r\) and \(s\) have a common \(1\)-digit, consider the least binary position where this happens. There is no carry into that position, because below it there is no position where both digits are \(1\). At the chosen position, adding the two \(1\)'s makes the corresponding digit of \(r+s\) equal to \(0\), whereas the digit of \(s\) is \(1\). Thus (1) fails. This establishes (2).

We now expand the generating function. For each fixed \(n\), the binomial theorem and the negative-binomial expansion give
\[
(1+x^n)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^{nk}
\]
and
\[
\frac1{(1-x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}\binom{n+j}{j}x^{(n+1)j}.
\]
Therefore
\[
x^n\frac{(1+x^n)^n}{(1-x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
 =\sum_{k=0}^n\sum_{j\ge0}
   \binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
   x^{n(k+1)+j(n+1)}.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(N)=
\sum_{\substack{n,k,j\ge0\\k\le n\\
 n(k+1)+j(n+1)=N}}
\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}.
\tag{3}
\]
This is a finite sum: the displayed exponent equation implies \(n\le N\), and for each \(n,k\) it determines at most one \(j\).

Since we only care about (3) modulo \(2\), define \(S_N\) to be the finite set of triples \((n,k,j)\) of nonnegative integers satisfying
\[
k\le n,
\tag{4}
\]
\[
n(k+1)+j(n+1)=N,
\tag{5}
\]
and
\[
\binom nk\text{ is odd},\qquad
\binom{n+j}{j}\text{ is odd}.
\tag{6}
\]
Each summand in (3) is odd exactly when both binomial factors are odd. Hence all triples not in \(S_N\) contribute \(0\) modulo \(2\), while every triple in \(S_N\) contributes \(1\). Thus
\[
a(N)\equiv |S_N|\pmod 2.
\tag{7}
\]

We construct an involution on \(S_N\). Take \((n,k,j)\in S_N\), and put
\[
q=n-k.
\]
This is nonnegative by (4), and \(n=q+k\). Since
\[
\binom nk=\binom{q+k}{k}
\]
is odd, criterion (2) gives
\[
q\perp k.
\tag{8}
\]
Likewise, because \(\binom{n+j}{j}\) is odd, (2) gives
\[
n\perp j.
\tag{9}
\]
Because \(n=q+k\) and \(q\perp k\), the sum \(q+k\) has no carries and is the bitwise OR of \(q\) and \(k\). Condition (9) therefore says that \(j\) has no common \(1\)-digit with either \(q\) or \(k\). In particular,
\[
j\perp k,
\qquad
j\perp q.
\tag{10}
\]
From \(j\perp k\), the sum \(j+k\) also has no carries. Since both \(j\) and \(k\) are binary-disjoint from \(q\), it follows that
\[
(j+k)\perp q.
\tag{11}
\]

Define
\[
\Phi(n,k,j)=(j+k,\ k,\ q)=(j+k,\ k,\ n-k).
\tag{12}
\]
We verify carefully that this is again an element of \(S_N\).

First, \(k\le j+k\), so the analogue of (4) holds. Second, the two required binomial coefficients are
\[
\binom{j+k}{k}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{(j+k)+q}{q}.
\]
The first is odd by \(j\perp k\), and the second is odd by \((j+k)\perp q\), using (2) in both cases.

It remains to check the exponent equation. Replacing \(n\) by \(q+k\), the original equation (5) is
\[
N=(q+k)(k+1)+j(q+k+1).
\tag{13}
\]
Expanding and regrouping its right-hand side gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(q+k)(k+1)+j(q+k+1)
 &=qk+q+k(k+1)+jq+jk+j\\
 &=(j+k)(k+1)+q(j+k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
N=(j+k)(k+1)+q((j+k)+1),
\]
which is precisely the exponent equation for the new triple \((j+k,k,q)\). Therefore \(\Phi\) maps \(S_N\) into itself.

The map \(\Phi\) is an involution. Indeed, for the new first coordinate \(n'=j+k\), subtracting its second coordinate gives
\[
n'-k=(j+k)-k=j.
\]
Consequently, applying (12) a second time yields
\[
\Phi(j+k,k,q)=(q+k,k,j)=(n,k,j).
\tag{14}
\]
Thus every non-fixed element of \(S_N\) is paired with one distinct partner.

We next determine what a fixed point can look like. Suppose that \((n,k,j)\in S_N\) is fixed by \(\Phi\). Equality of the first coordinates in (12) gives
\[
n=j+k.
\tag{15}
\]
The oddness of \(\binom nk=\binom{j+k}{k}\), together with (2), implies
\[
j\perp k.
\tag{16}
\]
Hence the addition in (15) has no carries: in binary, \(n\) is the bitwise OR of \(j\) and \(k\). In particular, every \(1\)-digit of \(j\) is also a \(1\)-digit of \(n\).

On the other hand, the oddness of \(\binom{n+j}{j}\), again by (2), says
\[
n\perp j.
\tag{17}
\]
Conditions (15)--(17) force \(j=0\): if \(j\) had any \(1\)-digit, that digit would also occur in \(n\), contradicting \(n\perp j\). Thus \(j=0\), and (15) then gives
\[
n=k.
\]
Substituting these values into the exponent equation (5), we obtain
\[
N=n(k+1)+j(n+1)=k(k+1).
\tag{18}
\]
Therefore every fixed point of \(\Phi\) forces \(N\) to have the required form.

Finally, suppose that \(a(N)\) is odd. By (7), the finite set \(S_N\) has odd cardinality. A finite set equipped with an involution is the disjoint union of its fixed points and two-element orbits. Since the two-element orbits contribute an even number of elements, an odd-cardinality set must contain a fixed point. Applying (18) to such a fixed point produces a nonnegative integer \(k\) with
\[
N=k(k+1).
\]
This proves that odd terms of the sequence can occur only at indices of the stated form.
